description: we are a high school student team who explores space data to build fun
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is an environmental investigation platform that helps people understand how our planet is changing through satellite imagery, historical data, graphs, and explanations.

The project focuses on answering three important questions:
- What is changing on Earth?
- Where is the change happening?
- Why does it matter?
Main features
1. Global Change Explorer: Explore different environmental changes and their locations around the world.
2. Environmental Investigations: Study five real-world cases:
   - Amazon Rainforest – deforestation
   - Lake Mead – shrinking water levels
   - Lake Kariba – water-level changes
   - Pareechu Landslide Lake – historical flood event
   - Forest Fires – fire monitoring
3. Satellite Image Comparison: Compare images from different dates to understand environmental changes.
4. Trend Analyzer: Explore historical environmental measurements using graphs.
5. Detective Report: Generate reports containing investigation findings, evidence, and sources.
Main objective
Our goal is to make complex Earth observation information easier for students, educators, and the public to understand.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Earth Trend Detective is an interactive web platform that helps ordinary people discover, compare and understand environmental change seen from space. It has five curated investigations: Amazon deforestation, Lake Mead, Lake Kariba, the Pareechu landslide lake in Tibet, and global fire detections. Each investigation follows the same steps:

  • Global Explorer: a map where users filter by category (forest, water level, flood, drought, fire) and pick an event.
  • Comparison: a before-and-after slider over real satellite imagery (for the Amazon, Landsat scenes from 2001 and 2019).
  • Investigation: structured answers to what happened, where, when, what evidence supports it, possible causes, why it matters, and scientific caveats.
  • Trend Analyzer: graphs of published historical measurements, such as Amazon clearing falling from over 20,000 km² a year to about 5,000 km² by 2012.
  • Detective Report: a printable report with findings, impacts, measurements and source links that users can save as a PDF.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns raw Earth observation data into a guided story anyone can follow, with no GIS skills needed.
  • It teaches people to treat satellite data as evidence. Every case lists its caveats, for example that tree-cover loss is not the same as confirmed illegal deforestation.
  • It is fast and free to use. It needs no sign-in and no live data feeds that could break.
  • Every claim credits its source (NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat/USGS, MODIS, INPE PRODES, FIRMS).

What is the intended impact?
We want more people, including students, teachers, journalists and community members, to understand how the planet is changing and why it matters, and to feel able to look at the evidence themselves. Understanding change is a first step toward protecting the environment. Our tagline is “Every Pixel Tells a Story. Every Change Matters.”

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages and hosting: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, deployed on Vercel. The map is built with local SVG, not a live map service.
  • Data and imagery: NASA Earth Observatory stories, Landsat (USGS), MODIS and ASTER imagery, NASA Blue Marble, FIRMS fire detection data, and the INPE PRODES clearing figures that NASA cites. All are bundled locally as curated assets.

How is it creative?

  • It frames environmental data as a detective investigation, with clues, evidence and a final report. Most Earth data tools are built for scientists, not for curious beginners.
  • One consistent structure across five very different events (forest, reservoirs, a landslide lake, fires) lets users compare cases and build a skill, not just read a result.
  • The printable report turns viewing into something the user produces, which suits classroom and community use.
  • We are open about what it is: a curated demonstration, not a live monitoring system. That honesty is part of the design.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: plain language, a clear five-step flow, and a layout that works for non-experts.
  • Scientific accuracy: we used only published NASA-sourced figures and added caveats to each case. Fire detections are presented as a starting clue, not a verdict.
  • Reliability: we used static, curated assets so the demo works offline-friendly and doesn’t depend on live APIs during judging.
  • Scope: we chose five strong case studies over broad but shallow coverage, and plan to add live data later.
  • Credit and ethics: every image and dataset is credited to its source.
